source_boundary.preserved_question_intent: Compare Java Thread.sleep and Object.wait, especially monitor ownership/release, wake-up conditions, intended use and interruption behavior, without expanding into unrelated thread-state trivia or claiming scheduler timing guarantees.

sources.title: Java SE 26 Thread API: sleep
anchors: Thread.sleep is static and causes the currently executing thread to sleep for the requested duration subject to timer/scheduler precision
sleep does not lose ownership of any monitors
interruption while sleeping throws InterruptedException and clears the interrupted status

sources.title: Java SE 26 Object API: wait/notify/notifyAll
anchors: the current thread must own the object's monitor before calling wait or IllegalMonitorStateException is thrown
wait puts the thread in this object's wait set and relinquishes synchronization claims on this object only; other object monitors remain held
wait can return due to notification, interruption, timeout or spurious wakeup and the API recommends checking the condition in a while loop
after notification a waiter still must reacquire the object's monitor before proceeding
interrupted wait throws InterruptedException and clears interrupted status after the object's lock status is restored

sources.title: Java Language Specification 26 §17.2 Wait Sets and Notification
anchors: every object has an associated monitor and wait set
wait and interruption/notification actions have defined ordering and monitor reacquisition behavior

claims.text: Thread.sleep does not require owning an object's monitor and does not release monitors the current thread already owns. Object.wait must be invoked by a thread that owns that object's monitor; it enters that object's wait set and releases synchronization claims on that object only, while other monitors remain held.

sleep is primarily duration-based and becomes eligible to continue after the requested sleep period subject to scheduler/timer behavior or interruption. wait is condition/notification-oriented and may return due to notify/notifyAll, interruption, timeout on timed wait, or spurious wakeup; after wake-up it must reacquire the object's monitor before continuing.

Because Object.wait can wake spuriously and notification does not itself prove the application condition is true, condition waiting should check the predicate in a while loop around wait rather than using wait as a one-shot event flag.

Both sleep and wait are interruptible and throw InterruptedException under their documented interruption conditions; the interrupted status is cleared when that exception is thrown. For wait, the object monitor is reacquired/restored before InterruptedException is delivered as specified.

Use sleep for deliberate timing/backoff/delay when holding monitors is not part of a coordination protocol. Use wait/notify only as monitor-based condition coordination while owning the monitor and protecting a predicate; for larger concurrency designs, higher-level java.util.concurrent constructs may provide clearer ownership and cancellation semantics, but that is an engineering selection boundary rather than a different definition of sleep/wait.

writer_constraints: Lead with the monitor-release distinction but state it precisely: sleep releases no monitors; wait releases the monitor of the object on which wait is invoked, not every lock held by the thread.
State that wait belongs to Object, not Thread, and requires the current thread to own the target object's monitor; otherwise IllegalMonitorStateException is thrown.
Do not say notify immediately makes the waiting thread execute. A notified waiter must reacquire the object's monitor and compete before proceeding.
Do not promise exact sleep wake-up timing. The duration is subject to system timer/scheduler precision and the thread still needs scheduling after the sleep period.
Explain spurious wakeups and the API-recommended while-loop predicate pattern for wait.
Cover interruption for both methods and avoid the common oversimplification that one is interruptible and the other is not.
Keep thread-state labels secondary; answer the frozen comparison through purpose, owner, monitor behavior, wake conditions and use cases.
Do not fabricate project incidents or performance numbers.
